activities.caption: drag the divider across the redesign
activities.name: sqlBigtableCompare

config.prompt: Same school register, two shapes — drag the divider:

before.label: one big table
before.text: Reads fine, joins look like extra work — and the tutor's room changes while 400 rows need editing; a student with no courses cannot exist; cancelling a last enrolment erases the student.

after.label: normalised schema
after.text: Each fact stored once so the tables cannot disagree with themselves — the join you pay at query time is cheap and automatic.

config.why: A small, predictable price for eliminating a whole class of silent corruption — normalise by default, denormalise deliberately for measured performance.

config.prompt: File each behaviour under the join that does it:

items.label: matches rows on the keys and drops non-matches
keeps all left rows, fills missing right rows with NULL
customers with no orders this year disappear
the single most useful join distinction

config.why: One declarative sentence; the engine chooses scan or index, join order and hash versus nested loops.

activities.caption: which curve is the indexed lookup?
activities.name: sqlIndexTrace

config.prompt: Rows touched against data size — which curve is lookup by a highly varied key on a B-tree?
config.why: With a highly varied key the planner touches 3–4 nodes instead of millions of rows; with 6 distinct values, each entry still points at a sixth of the store — barely better than reading everything.

activities.anchor: which is why one busy PostgreSQL database can serve thousands of simultaneous sessions honestly
activities.caption: walk the isolation dial
activities.name: sqlIsoBranch

config.root: Two sessions run against the same account table. Walk the concurrency choices.

start.text: Session A reads a balance that Session B has written but not yet committed. What just happened?

choices.label: A dirty read — A may act on data that gets rolled back
choices.feedback: Exactly the anomaly isolation exists to prevent — READ UNCOMMITTED allows it; production engines usually refuse.

choices.label: Nothing yet — commits will sort it out
choices.feedback: If B rolls back, A has already acted on money that never moved — the bug isolation prevents.

dirty.text: You need isolation. Which level, at what cost?

choices.label: READ COMMITTED — never see uncommitted data
choices.feedback: The common production floor: each read sees committed data only, trading some anomaly risk for concurrency.

choices.label: SERIALIZABLE — as if transactions ran one at a time
choices.feedback: Maximum safety, minimum concurrency — the dial runs from READ UNCOMMITTED up to here.

later.text: If B rolls back, A has acted on money that never moved — the dirty read is why isolation is a guarantee, not a courtesy.

rc.text: READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ: production trade-offs — anomaly risk priced against concurrency, delivered by locking or MVCC (readers never block writers).

serial.text: SERIALIZABLE: the strictest rung — safest books, least throughput; the dial is a spectrum, not a switch.

config.why: Isolation is a range, not a binary — production systems trade anomaly risk for concurrency, and MVCC lets readers never block writers.

activities.caption: from spreadsheet to schema, in order
activities.name: sqlMigrateOrder

config.prompt: From spreadsheet to schema — put the moves in order:
items: Identify entities — students, tutors, courses, enrolments: the nouns with their own identity
Move attributes to the entity they describe — dob to students, room to tutors
Model the relationship as its own table — enrolments(student_id, course_id, grade)
Four tables joined by foreign keys — update-proof by construction
config.why: The tutor's room exists once; history is preserved; the 'who takes what' view is one join away.

activities.anchor: constraints turn business rules into database-enforced facts
activities.caption: pair each tool with the rule it enforces
activities.name: sqlConstraintMatch

config.prompt: Pair each tool with the rule it enforces:

pairs.right: 'create or refresh' as one atomic statement — no read-then-write race

config.why: The schema is policy: a well-typed table partly enforces its own correctness, surviving the next developer who has not read your comments.

activities.anchor: pricing arithmetic in floats accumulates errors that audits find and courts punish
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the type consequences
activities.name: sqlTypeSpot

config.prompt: One of these type choices is wrong — click it:
lines: Money in DECIMAL: binary representation makes 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004.
Dates as DATE, not strings: a typed DATE gives range queries, indexing and arithmetic for free.
A status column typed as an enumerated set makes invalid states unrepresentable.
CHAR vs VARCHAR: a two-letter country code wants VARCHAR(2) for flexibility.
Types are the cheapest constraints you will ever buy — enforced at every insert, no application code.
config.correction: Fixed vs variable text trades padding for flexibility — a two-letter country code wants CHAR(2), the fixed-width type.
config.why: Types are the cheapest constraints you will ever buy — schema is policy.

activities.anchor: The planner estimates selectivities from statistics
activities.caption: call the size of the planner's search
activities.name: sqlPlannerEst

config.prompt: For a join across 8 tables, roughly how many possible orderings must the optimiser enumerate?
config.why: About 17,000 — heuristics required; a 'fast query' is really 'a plan that could be estimated well'.
config.context: Stale metadata is the classic cause of sudden slowness.
